title: Why a work message can feel like a threat
performance: the next time a message spikes their stress, the viewer names it as the body's alarm and takes a short pause before replying

audience.assumed_prior: has felt a racing heart before a tough email; no physiology
audience.why: the brief's audience is office staff in any role; the knowledge sheet assumes no prior terms
audience.motivation: voluntary; wants to stay clear-headed when work gets tense
audience.context: laptop or phone, often muted, so captions and on-screen labels carry the terms

strategy.name: scenario_led
strategy.rationale: one ordinary moment at a desk carries the whole mechanism, so every idea is seen happening to someone before it is named
strategy.signature_move: freeze one worker's moment, open it up to show the alarm running inside her, then replay the moment with a pause

misconceptions.belief: a strong reaction to an email means I am overreacting or bad at my job
misconceptions.why_tempting: nothing physical is happening, so the racing heart feels out of proportion

hook.sketch: Say a message lands marked urgent. Before you have read the second line, your heart is already racing. Why?

arc.promise: in one minute: what that alarm is, and one move that helps
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 starts from the racing heart every viewer has felt before a tough message

sections.goal: the viewer can explain what the fast stress response does in the body
sections.carrier: the worker lit from inside, labels pinned to her body as each hormone is named, a status panel whose slower jobs switch off one per word

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a message can set off an alarm built for physical danger
sections.carrier: a burst behind her at the moment of alarm, then the pressures of the day closing in around her

sections.goal: the viewer can use a short pause before replying to a message that set off the alarm
sections.carrier: the same desk replayed calm: the alarm settles, the reply goes out on purpose

arc.payoff: the same urgent message again: this time she notices the alarm, pauses, and replies on purpose

practice_ladder.what: the worker notices the alarm, pauses, then replies
the viewer is asked to try one pause on their next tense message

slowdown_at: why a message sets off the alarm

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: So that racing heart is not a fault. It is the alarm doing its job, a little too well.

transfer_tasks: on your next tense message, notice the alarm and take one slow pause before you reply

persona.voice: the mentor persona: a calm colleague who has felt this too
persona.delivery_notes: quick and close in the hook, slower on why a message sets the alarm off, warm on the last line

gagne.attention: hook: the urgent message and the racing heart
gagne.objective: promise: what the alarm is and one move that helps
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 starts from the racing heart the viewer has felt
gagne.present: sections in order: what it does, why it fires, what to do
gagne.guidance: signature move: freeze the moment, open it up, replay it
gagne.feedback: the replay shows the alarm settling after the pause
gagne.transfer: transfer task: one pause on the next tense message

merrill.problem_centered: one worker's urgent message is the running problem
merrill.activation: sec1 opens from the viewer's own racing heart
merrill.demonstration: the alarm is shown running inside her before it is named
merrill.integration: the transfer task puts it in the viewer's next tense message

mayer.coherence: one worker, one metaphor (an alarm), no side stories
mayer.signalling: one slowdown on why a message sets the alarm off
mayer.redundancy: screen shows labels and the status panel; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each label appears as it is spoken
mayer.segmenting: three short sections, one idea each
mayer.pre_training: the alarm is named before the hormones

arcs.relevance: every office worker has felt this
